collection.title: Social Media and Its Effects on People and Society: An Annotated Research Collection (2026 edition)
collection.summary: The research shows that social media's effects are real but usually smaller and more conditional than public debate suggests. Harms concentrate in heavy, compulsive ("addictive") use, in vulnerable subgroups such as early-adolescent girls, and in specific design features like engagement-ranked feeds. The best causal studies of average effects on polarization and population-level mental health mostly find small effects. This collection lists 83 papers and reports grouped by theme, each with a citation, DOI or link, design, sample and key finding. It gives most weight to influential and 2020–2026 work and flags where scholars disagree.
tldr: Mental health: Correlations between total time on social media and youth depression or anxiety are consistent but small (Orben & Przybylski 2019 found technology use explains 0.4% of variance in adolescent well-being). Newer cohort studies point to addictive use, not hours, as the stronger risk signal: Xiao et al. 2025 in JAMA found 2–3× higher risk of suicidal behaviour. Whether reducing social media use improves mental health is still contested among meta-analyses (Ferguson 2024 null; Thrul et al. 2025 and Veber Lopes et al. 2026 positive).

Politics: The 2020 Meta–academic studies in Science, Nature and PNAS found that changing Facebook/Instagram feeds or deactivating accounts during an election changed what people saw but not polarization. Newer independent experiments on X (Gauthier et al. 2026 in Nature; Piccardi et al. 2025 in Science) show feed algorithms can shift attitudes and partisan animosity. "No effect" claims about algorithms therefore do not generalize across platforms.

Policy: Evidence for bans is weak so far. Australia's under-16 law left more than 8 in 10 under-16s still using restricted platforms after three months (BMJ 2026; eSafety 2026). UK school phone restrictions showed no wellbeing benefit (SMART Schools 2025). Design-level changes (feed reranking, accuracy prompts, prebunking) and voluntary reduction have stronger experimental support than access bans.
key_findings: The "how much" matters less than the "how." The strongest recent evidence ties harm to compulsive patterns and specific mechanisms: addictive use (#14, #26, #27), sleep displacement (#25), harassment (#11, #62) and appearance comparison (#17, #24). Policies aimed only at time limits will likely underperform those aimed at compulsive design.

Causal evidence for mental health harm exists but is modest. The Facebook college rollout (#17) and deactivation RCTs (#18, #19) show effects of roughly 0.04–0.1 SD: meaningful at population scale, but far from explaining the entire rise in youth distress. Neither the "moral panic" nor the "proven epidemic cause" camp is fully supported. The experimental meta-analyses (#21–#23) lean slightly toward benefits from reducing use, especially for interventions of 2–3 weeks or longer.

The politics literature has shifted since 2023. The 2020 Meta studies (#40–#44) found near-zero attitudinal effects from changing Meta's feeds for a few months, but independent 2025–2026 experiments on X (#46, #47) show algorithms and ranking objectives can move attitudes and animosity. Effects are platform-, period- and design-specific.

Misinformation is highly concentrated. False news spreads faster (#34), but exposure and sharing concentrate in small, older, highly partisan subgroups (#35, #36), so targeted interventions are more efficient than population-wide alarm.

People are trapped, not just hooked. Users value access individually yet many would prefer the platforms not exist (#64, #65). This supports coordinated policy (school norms, defaults, age rules) over individual willpower, provided it can be enforced.

Bans are not yet working as designed. Australia's law has been widely circumvented at three months (#72, #73) and UK school phone evidence is null for wellbeing (#75); design-level interventions (7b) have better experimental support so far.
caveats: Correlational dominance: Most mental health and short-form video studies are correlational and rely on self-reported use. A preregistered meta-analysis of 106 effect sizes (Parry et al. 2021, Nature Human Behaviour) found that self-reported use "correlates only moderately with logged measurements," and that problematic-use scales track usage logs even more weakly.

Platform partnerships: The 2020 Meta studies were run with Meta's cooperation under independent-researcher control agreements. Critics (Bagchi et al. 2024, Science eLetter) point to 63 emergency "break-glass" changes Meta made to Facebook's feed algorithm at the same time. The X studies (#46, #47) avoided platform cooperation but had smaller samples or shorter durations.
Preprints and working papers: #19, #23, #65 and #81 are not (or not yet) peer-reviewed journal articles; treat them as provisional.
Contested numbers: Haidt/Twenge and Orben/Przybylski/Odgers/Ferguson disagree on the same data; judge effect sizes against benchmarks (e.g., 0.05–0.1 SD) rather than headlines.
Citation details: A few DOIs and page ranges for older papers come from standard bibliographic records and should be verified before formal citation; #26 is listed without a DOI.
collection.gaps: eSafety's 6-, 12- and 24-month waves; peer review of #23; independent replications of the X algorithm findings; rigorous causal work on the creator economy and AI-generated content.

themes.name: Mental health & wellbeing
themes.strength: Large, mostly correlational; growing experimental base
themes.bottom_line: Small average associations; stronger for girls, early adolescence, and addictive use. Causal direction partly established (Braghieri et al. 2022; Nagata et al. 2025), magnitude disputed.

themes.name: Attention, cognition & behavior
themes.bottom_line: Short-form video and compulsive checking are linked to poorer attention and inhibitory control. Causal evidence is thin, apart from smartphone-blocking RCTs.

themes.name: Politics & democracy
themes.bottom_line: Falsehoods spread faster than truth. Echo chambers exist but are smaller than feared. X's algorithm shifted attitudes; Meta-feed changes in 2020 did not.

themes.name: Social relationships & society
themes.bottom_line: Builds bridging social capital and enables collective action. Cyberbullying is linked to poorer mental health, though offline victimisation explains much of that link.

themes.name: Economic & information ecosystem
themes.strength: Strong welfare experiments; descriptive news data
themes.bottom_line: Users value access individually but may prefer a world without the platforms ("collective traps"). Platform news withdrawals sharply cut news reach. Creator-economy causal evidence is sparse.

themes.name: Positive effects
themes.bottom_line: Peer support, identity and community benefits are real, especially for LGBTQ+ and isolated youth; evidence quality is weaker.

themes.name: Policy & interventions
themes.bottom_line: Bans circumvented so far; school phone restrictions show null wellbeing effects; design and literacy interventions show modest gains; DSA transparency audits find large compliance gaps.

designs.name: Randomized experiment
designs.can_show: cause, for the people in the sample, the platform and period studied, and the length of the intervention

designs.name: Natural experiment
designs.can_show: cause, if the as-good-as-random assumption holds (say what it is and how it was tested)

designs.name: Cohort and longitudinal
designs.can_show: what comes before what, and within-person change; not cause on its own (confounders can still drive both)

designs.name: Observational and platform data
designs.can_show: association, prevalence and spread; not cause

designs.name: Meta-analysis and review
designs.can_show: what the studies it pools show together; no stronger than the designs it pools (say which it pooled)

designs.name: Report and commentary
designs.can_show: an institution's or an expert's reading of the evidence: attribute it, and trace its claims to the studies behind them

studies.label: Twenge et al. 2018
studies.authors: Twenge, J. M., Joiner, T. E., Rogers, M. L., & Martin, G. N.
studies.title: Increases in depressive symptoms, suicide-related outcomes, and suicide rates among U.S. adolescents after 2010 and links to increased new media screen time
studies.citation: Twenge, J. M., Joiner, T. E., Rogers, M. L., & Martin, G. N. (2018). Increases in depressive symptoms, suicide-related outcomes, and suicide rates among U.S. adolescents after 2010 and links to increased new media screen time. Clinical Psychological Science, 6(1), 3–17.
studies.type_sample: Repeated cross-sectional trend analysis; Monitoring the Future and YRBSS (more than 500,000 adolescents).
studies.findings: Depressive symptoms and suicide-related outcomes rose after 2010, especially among girls, in step with smartphone and social media adoption. Foundational, but correlational at the population level.

studies.label: Orben & Przybylski 2019
studies.authors: Orben, A., & Przybylski, A. K.
studies.title: The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use
studies.citation: Orben, A., & Przybylski, A. K. (2019). The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use. Nature Human Behaviour, 3, 173–182.
studies.type_sample: Specification-curve analysis; more than 355,000 adolescents (US and UK).
studies.findings: Digital technology use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being, comparable to eating potatoes. The landmark "small effects" paper.
studies.note: The landmark "small effects" paper, and one side of the field's central dispute: #3 re-analyses the same data and finds larger associations for girls and social media specifically. Put both on the page.

studies.label: Twenge et al. 2022
studies.authors: Twenge, J. M., Haidt, J., Lozano, J., & Cummins, K. M.
studies.title: Specification curve analysis shows that social media use is linked to poor mental health, especially among girls
studies.citation: Twenge, J. M., Haidt, J., Lozano, J., & Cummins, K. M. (2022). Specification curve analysis shows that social media use is linked to poor mental health, especially among girls. Acta Psychologica, 224, 103512.
studies.type_sample: Re-analysis of the same datasets as #2.
studies.findings: Isolating social media (not all screen time) and girls yields substantially larger associations. The direct rebuttal to #2, showing how analytic choices drive conclusions.
studies.note: A direct rebuttal of #2 on the same datasets: the disagreement is about analytic choices. Put both on the page.

studies.label: Orben et al. 2022
studies.authors: Orben, A., Przybylski, A. K., Blakemore, S.-J., & Kievit, R. A.
studies.title: Windows of developmental sensitivity to social media
studies.citation: Orben, A., Przybylski, A. K., Blakemore, S.-J., & Kievit, R. A. (2022). Windows of developmental sensitivity to social media. Nature Communications, 13, 1649.
studies.type_sample: Longitudinal cohort; about 17,400 UK participants aged 10–80.
studies.findings: Higher use predicted lower later life satisfaction at specific ages (about 11–13 for girls, 14–15 for boys, 19 for both), suggesting sensitive developmental windows rather than uniform harm.

studies.label: Odgers 2024
studies.authors: Odgers, C. L.
studies.title: The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?
studies.citation: Odgers, C. L. (2024). The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness? Nature, 628, 29–30.
studies.type_sample: Expert review of Haidt's The Anxious Generation (2024).
studies.findings: Argues "there is no evidence that using these platforms is rewiring children's brains or driving an epidemic of mental illness," pointing to alternative causes such as post-2008 economic stress. Haidt replied on his After Babel Substack (not peer-reviewed), citing experimental evidence. Read the two together.

studies.authors: Valkenburg, P. M., Meier, A., & Beyens, I.
studies.title: Social media use and its impact on adolescent mental health: An umbrella review of the evidence
studies.citation: Valkenburg, P. M., Meier, A., & Beyens, I. (2022). Social media use and its impact on adolescent mental health: An umbrella review of the evidence. Current Opinion in Psychology, 44, 58–68.
studies.type_sample: Umbrella review.
studies.findings: Reviews interpret the same weak-to-moderate associations very differently. Effects are heterogeneous: most adolescents show no effect, minorities show positive or negative effects.

studies.label: Beyens et al. 2020
studies.authors: Beyens, I., Pouwels, J. L., van Driel, I. I., Keijsers, L., & Valkenburg, P. M.
studies.title: The effect of social media on well-being differs from adolescent to adolescent
studies.citation: Beyens, I., Pouwels, J. L., van Driel, I. I., Keijsers, L., & Valkenburg, P. M. (2020). The effect of social media on well-being differs from adolescent to adolescent. Scientific Reports, 10, 10763.
studies.type_sample: Experience sampling; 63 adolescents, 34,930 assessments.
studies.findings: 46% felt better after passive use, 10% felt worse, the rest showed no effect. Key evidence for "person-specific" effects.

studies.label: U.S. Surgeon General 2023
studies.authors: U.S. Surgeon General
studies.title: Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory
studies.citation: U.S. Surgeon General (2023). Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory. HHS.
studies.findings: Up to 95% of US 13–17-year-olds use social media; those using more than 3 hours/day face double the risk of depression and anxiety symptoms. Concludes there is not enough evidence to call social media safe for youth, while noting benefits for marginalized youth such as LGBTQ+ peer support.

studies.label: National Academies 2024
studies.authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
studies.title: Social Media and Adolescent Health
studies.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2024). Social Media and Adolescent Health. National Academies Press.
studies.findings: The evidence does not support the conclusion that social media causes population-level changes in adolescent mental health. Still recommends platform design standards, age-appropriate defaults and more researcher data access. The most cautious major review.

studies.label: APA 2023
studies.authors: American Psychological Association
studies.title: Health Advisory on Social Media Use in Adolescence
studies.citation: American Psychological Association (2023). Health Advisory on Social Media Use in Adolescence.
studies.findings: Social media is "not inherently beneficial or harmful"; risks depend on content, features (infinite scroll, likes) and displacement of sleep and activity. Recommends monitoring in early adolescence.

studies.label: Kelly et al. 2018
studies.authors: Kelly, Y., Zilanawala, A., Booker, C., & Sacker, A.
studies.title: Social media use and adolescent mental health: Findings from the UK Millennium Cohort Study
studies.citation: Kelly, Y., Zilanawala, A., Booker, C., & Sacker, A. (2018). Social media use and adolescent mental health: Findings from the UK Millennium Cohort Study. EClinicalMedicine, 6, 59–68.
studies.type_sample: Cohort; about 11,000 UK 14-year-olds.
studies.findings: Heavier use was associated with more depressive symptoms, more strongly in girls, largely accounted for by online harassment, poor sleep, low self-esteem and poor body image.

studies.label: Riehm et al. 2019
studies.authors: Riehm, K. E., Feder, K. A., Tormohlen, K. N., et al.
studies.title: Associations between time spent using social media and internalizing and externalizing problems among US youth
studies.citation: Riehm, K. E., Feder, K. A., Tormohlen, K. N., et al. (2019). Associations between time spent using social media and internalizing and externalizing problems among US youth. JAMA Psychiatry, 76(12), 1266–1273.
studies.type_sample: Prospective cohort (PATH); 6,595 US adolescents.
studies.findings: More than 3 hours/day predicted elevated risk of later internalizing problems; the main source for the Surgeon General's "3 hours" threshold.

studies.label: Nagata et al. 2025
studies.authors: Nagata, J. M., Otmar, C. D., Shim, J., et al.
studies.title: Social media use and depressive symptoms during early adolescence
studies.citation: Nagata, J. M., Otmar, C. D., Shim, J., et al. (2025). Social media use and depressive symptoms during early adolescence. JAMA Network Open, 8(5), e2511704.
studies.type_sample: Prospective cohort, within-person cross-lagged models; about 11,900 US children (ABCD Study), ages 9–13.
studies.findings: Within-person increases in use predicted higher depressive symptoms the next year (β = 0.07–0.09); depressive symptoms did not predict later use. Between-person differences were not significant after adjustment: real but small effects.

studies.label: Xiao et al. 2025
studies.authors: Xiao, Y., Meng, Y., Brown, T. T., Keyes, K. M., & Mann, J. J.
studies.title: Addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, and mental health in US youths
studies.citation: Xiao, Y., Meng, Y., Brown, T. T., Keyes, K. M., & Mann, J. J. (2025). Addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, and mental health in US youths. JAMA, 334(3), 219–228.
studies.type_sample: Prospective cohort (ABCD), trajectory modeling; about 4,300 youths over 4 years.
studies.findings: Nearly one-third followed an increasing addictive social-media-use trajectory from age 11. High or increasing addictive use was associated with 2–3× higher risk of suicidal behaviors and ideation (risk ratio 2.14 for increasing addictive social media use); total screen time was not. Shifts focus from "time" to "compulsive use."

studies.label: Shakya & Christakis 2017
studies.authors: Shakya, H. B., & Christakis, N. A.
studies.title: Association of Facebook use with compromised well-being: A longitudinal study
studies.citation: Shakya, H. B., & Christakis, N. A. (2017). Association of Facebook use with compromised well-being: A longitudinal study. American Journal of Epidemiology, 185(3), 203–211.
studies.type_sample: Three-wave longitudinal; 5,208 US adults (Gallup).
studies.findings: Liking others' content and clicking links predicted later declines in self-reported physical and mental health and life satisfaction; real-world networks had the opposite association.

studies.label: Kross et al. 2013
studies.authors: Kross, E., Verduyn, P., Demiralp, E., et al.
studies.title: Facebook use predicts declines in subjective well-being in young adults
studies.citation: Kross, E., Verduyn, P., Demiralp, E., et al. (2013). Facebook use predicts declines in subjective well-being in young adults. PLOS ONE, 8(8), e69841.
studies.type_sample: Experience sampling; 82 young adults over 2 weeks.
studies.findings: More Facebook use predicted declines in momentary affect and in life satisfaction over time. A foundational early study.

studies.label: Braghieri et al. 2022
studies.authors: Braghieri, L., Levy, R., & Makarin, A.
studies.title: Social media and mental health
studies.citation: Braghieri, L., Levy, R., & Makarin, A. (2022). Social media and mental health. American Economic Review, 112(11), 3660–3693.
studies.type_sample: Natural experiment (staggered Facebook rollout across US colleges, 2004–2006); more than 430,000 National College Health Assessment responses.
studies.findings: Facebook's arrival worsened student mental health: severe depression rose about 7% and anxiety disorder about 20%, likely via unfavorable social comparison. Among the strongest causal designs.

studies.label: Allcott et al. 2020
studies.authors: Allcott, H., Braghieri, L., Eichmeyer, S., & Gentzkow, M.
studies.title: The welfare effects of social media
studies.citation: Allcott, H., Braghieri, L., Eichmeyer, S., & Gentzkow, M. (2020). The welfare effects of social media. American Economic Review, 110(3), 629–676.
studies.type_sample: Randomized 4-week deactivation before the 2018 midterms; 2,743 US Facebook users.
studies.findings: Deactivation increased offline activities, slightly improved well-being, reduced news knowledge and political polarization, and reduced later Facebook use. The landmark deactivation RCT.

studies.label: Allcott et al. 2025
studies.authors: Allcott, H., Gentzkow, M., Mason, W., et al.
studies.title: The effect of deactivating Facebook and Instagram on users' emotional state
studies.citation: Allcott, H., Gentzkow, M., Mason, W., et al. (2025). The effect of deactivating Facebook and Instagram on users' emotional state. NBER Working Paper 33697.
studies.type_sample: Large RCT (2020 Meta election studies); about 19,900 Facebook and 15,600 Instagram users.
studies.findings: Six weeks of Facebook deactivation improved a happiness/anxiety/depression index by 0.060 SD; Instagram by 0.041 SD, driven by women under 25 and not significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Real but small.

studies.authors: Hunt, M. G., Marx, R., Lipson, C., & Young, J.
studies.title: No more FOMO: Limiting social media decreases loneliness and depression
studies.venue: Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology
studies.citation: Hunt, M. G., Marx, R., Lipson, C., & Young, J. (2018). No more FOMO: Limiting social media decreases loneliness and depression. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 37(10), 751–768.
studies.type_sample: RCT; 143 US undergraduates.
studies.findings: Limiting Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to 10 minutes per platform per day (30 minutes total) for 3 weeks reduced loneliness and depression, especially among those more depressed at baseline. Widely cited; small sample.

studies.findings: Pooled effect d = 0.088 (p =.104), not different from zero; Ferguson argues this undermines causal claims that cutting social media would improve adolescent mental health. Contested: see #22–#23.

studies.findings: Ferguson mixed reduction with exposure studies and ignored intervention length; restricting to reduction/abstinence and modeling duration showed benefits, with an optimal length of about 3 weeks. studies.citation: Saiphoo, A. N., & Vahedi, Z. (2019). A meta-analytic review of the relationship between social media use and body image disturbance. Computers in Human Behavior, 101, 259–275.

studies.label: Alonzo et al. 2021
studies.authors: Alonzo, R., Hussain, J., Stranges, S., & Anderson, K. K.
studies.title: Interplay between social media use, sleep quality, and mental health in youth: A systematic review
studies.citation: Alonzo, R., Hussain, J., Stranges, S., & Anderson, K. K. (2021). Interplay between social media use, sleep quality, and mental health in youth: A systematic review. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 56, 101414.
studies.type_sample: Systematic review of 36 cross-sectional studies.
studies.findings: Excessive use is consistently associated with poor sleep quality, which is linked to depression and anxiety. Sleep is one of the best-supported mechanisms.

studies.label: Nguyen et al. 2025
studies.authors: Nguyen, L., Walters, J., Paul, S., Monreal Ijurco, S., Rainey, G. E., Parekh, N., Blair, G., & Darrah, M.
studies.title: Feeds, feelings, and focus: A systematic review and meta-analysis examining the cognitive and mental health correlates of short-form video use
studies.citation: Nguyen, L., Walters, J., Paul, S., Monreal Ijurco, S., Rainey, G. E., Parekh, N., Blair, G., & Darrah, M. (2025). Feeds, feelings, and focus: A systematic review and meta-analysis examining the cognitive and mental health correlates of short-form video use. Psychological Bulletin, 151(9), 1125–1146.
studies.type_sample: Meta-analysis; 71 studies, 98,299 participants.
studies.findings: Short-form video use was moderately associated with poorer cognition (r = −.34), especially attention (r = −.38) and inhibitory control (r = −.41), and weakly with poorer mental health (r = −.21), strongest for stress and anxiety; no association with body image or self-esteem. "Addictive" use drove effects more than duration. All included studies are correlational.

studies.findings: Users showed habit formation and self-control problems, which the authors estimate account for 31% of social media use: economic evidence that some use is behaviorally "addictive."
